patch.value: Contract-declared output ceilings are decorative on a real corpus: 10 of 30 read surfaces exceed their own declared token budget, the worst by 104x, and the gate that closed this defect measures a 27-item fixture

Every one of the 72 top-level commands declares a default_max_estimated_tokens in the contracts table, and on this workspace the declaration and the behaviour are unrelated numbers. Measured 2026-08-13 against 2,467 items with the shipped build, read-only default invocations, four bytes per estimated token.

Ten of thirty probed surfaces exceed their own declared ceiling. comments-audit declares 4,000 and emits 1,665,734 bytes for 416,433 tokens, a factor of 104. notes on pm-4k6b declares 2,000 and emits 62,596 tokens, a factor of 31. list declares 4,000 and emits 70,771, a factor of 17.7. health declares 6,000 and emits 30,552 by default, a factor of 5.1. comments declares 2,000 and emits 9,226, a factor of 4.6. deps declares 4,000 and emits 15,745, a factor of 3.9. events declares 4,000 and emits 9,199. history declares 4,000 and emits 5,767. search declares 4,000 and emits 4,414. Separately, assurance run against a real gate emits 502,068 bytes for roughly 125,517 tokens against a declared 4,000, a factor of 31, and that surface is the one hosted CI executes on every push.

For scale, the entire documented agent cold start is 29,479 bytes: context 9,505, next 9,491, contracts --summary 10,151. One assurance gate verdict therefore costs seventeen cold starts, and one comments-audit costs fifty-six.

The budget machinery exists and works. The same assurance run under --output-budget 500 returns 601 bytes, so the degradation path is implemented and simply is not the default, and nothing anywhere compares the emitted answer to the declared ceiling on a corpus that can exceed it.

Why the gate does not see this. scripts/release/token-budget-gate.mjs was shipped to close pm-9sui7t, whose finding was that the previous gate measured a three-item fixture. The replacement seeds SCALE_FIXTURE_ITEMS = 24 plus three, so the representative corpus is 27 items: 1.1 percent of this workspace and 0.0027 percent of the declared million-item target. More decisive than the item count is the shape. Every surface that overruns is priced by per-item collection depth rather than by item count, and the fixture models none of it: pm-doxj carries 138 notes and pm-4k6b carries 70, while the fixture's items carry a single comment each. comments-audit, the worst overrun in the product, is absent from the corpus entirely.

The class matters more than the instance. pm-9sui7t named the remedy precisely, which is that a gate must ship with a negative control proving it fails when the guarded property is violated. That gate does carry a negative control for an unbounded implementation, and it still cannot observe any of these ten overruns, because the negative control proves the comparison works and not that the corpus can trigger it. A fixture-bound gate answers the question 'does the comparison fire' and never the question 'does this product hold its contract'.

The output-budget corpus is measured against a workspace whose per-item collection depth is representative, not only its item count, and the corpus includes comments-audit, notes on a note-heavy item, assurance run, and bare list; A declared ceiling is enforced at runtime by default so a command degrades deterministically rather than exceeding its own contract; The gate's corpus adequacy is itself asserted, so a corpus that cannot trigger any known overrun fails the gate; The ten measured overruns are each either brought under their declared ceiling or have their ceiling re-declared with recorded rationale; list-closed and the other status aliases carry a declared ceiling
